> Limit is now calculated based on hardware, on my hardware it was ~270 decals. Do want to add a setting to limit this.

It makes sense to do this to reduce shader compilation times by default (which I think depend on the maximum total decal count supported), as well as ensuring the default works consistently on all hardware and platforms.

We should find a low-end mobile device to test this on, and use its limit as the default value for the project setting. This avoids surprises on export with some decals not appearing depending on the GPU.

cc @lawnjelly
Added a setting for it, for now put in on 64. We can tweak that more later when we get more feedback from people.
OK, @Calinou , so this issue: Is not related to the decals logic. It turns out to be the ReflectionProbe boundary on the water puddle example.

Ok, I did end up adding mipmap support and for this I've given the `decal_atlas` it's own texture. The existing `texture_atlas` is basically the same implementation but only used for canvas shaders. I didn't want to risk breaking that with changes.

`p_panorama_to_dp` is not supported on the decals, I believe this is used for light projectors, possibly something to look into at some future date.

Having quickly skimmed over the code, it seems you're using the `GL_LINEAR`/`GL_NEAREST` MIN filter modes. If I recall correctly, `textureGrad` requires the MIN filter to use the `_MIPMAP_` filtering modes.

Works great now :slightly_smiling_face: Nearest | Linear -|- | Nearest Mipmap | Linear Mipmap -|- | However, Nearest Mipmap Anisotropic and Linear Mipmap Anisotropic look the same as without anisotropic filtering, even though the anisotropic filter level is set to 16× in the Project Settings. I'm on NVIDIA for reference, which supports Nearest Mipmap Anisotropic (unlike AMD and Intel GPUs which either have to disable anisotropic filtering, or use linear filtering instead). Another difference with Forward+ is that the **Use Nearest Mipmap Filter** project setting does not affect decals, while it does affect other material rendereing in Compatibility (see the planes on the left which are regular MeshInstance3Ds, not decals): ### Forward+ https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9598b033-86b7-44cf-a4e9-63031fe4e53d ### Compatibility https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7f209b08-3cc8-4d46-ba5a-33b45538ec9e Notice the sudden mip transitions on the left on both meshes and decals in Forward+, but decals keep trilinear filtering in Compatibility regardless of the project setting. Lastly, this also occurs with nearest filter on decals, where **Use Nearest Mipmap Filter** is always trated as if it's enabled on decals in Compatibility, even if the setting is disabled: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e8088b26-f700-49b6-a0ee-083ec6538a58 In short, the value of **Use Nearest Mipmap Filter** should be used to determine whether bilinear or trilinear filtering is used, rather than the decal filter mode. **Updated testing project:** [test_pr_118070_2.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29516965/test_pr_118070_2.zip)

is there a reason for the 8 decal per surface limit? I'm working on a TD game that would benefit from decals but it doesn't make sense for me to split my small level into multiple chunks so that it works within that limit. I understand it might make sense for FPS bullet decals where each wall can be a seperate surface, but is it not possible to make the limit adjustable?

> is there a reason for the 8 decal per surface limit? I'm working on a TD game that would benefit from decals but it doesn't make sense for me to split my small level into multiple chunks so that it works within that limit. I understand it might make sense for FPS bullet decals where each wall can be a seperate surface, but is it not possible to make the limit adjustable?

It's a hard balance to make, it's the same argument with the light limits. It's more data to set before each drawcall, but more importantly, all the decals and lights attached to a surface will be evaluated for each fragment rendered for that surface, regardless of if that decal or light has an impact on that fragment. That is a lot of overhead and on a mobile renderer that is targeted at low end hardware, unforgivable overhead.

Breaking your large level into smaller chunks likely will have a lot of benefits performance wise, though it's always a tradeoff between more drawcalls v.s. more efficient fragment shading.

Thanks for the reply 🧡 I'm not targeting mobile, so if I were to increase the limit in a fork, is there anything I should be aware of for web and desktop? I'm probably looking at a max of 32 decals for the whole level, on the same surface which will be entirely drawn within the cameras frustrum most of the time. it's a stylised game with only one light, which is directional. 

or does 32 decals sound unreasonably expensive in this scenario? is the cost nonlinear vs 8?

> Thanks for the reply 🧡 I'm not targeting mobile, so if I were to increase the limit in a fork, is there anything I should be aware of for web and desktop? I'm probably looking at a max of 32 decals for the whole level, on the same surface which will be entirely drawn within the cameras frustrum most of the time. it's a stylised game with only one light, which is directional.
> 
> or does 32 decals sound unreasonably expensive in this scenario? is the cost nonlinear vs 8?

Hard one to judge, it all depends on how well the GPU can exit the loop early if you only have a few decals that effect a surface. We do use a different variant that removes decal logic all together if no decals are applied.

But it shouldn't be hard to increase the limit, just a matter of adding more uniforms that hold decal indices. You'll quickly find out if it has adverse effects.
If you have a large area with only a decal here and there, totalling up to 32, it's a lot of overhead looping through all 32 only to ignore most of them on each fragment.
It has all my alarm bells ringing, I would never go for something this wasteful in my own projects.

hi, i don't contribute to godot (yet) and i wanted to ask, if you have these limits in place for compatibility and mobile, how do you handle the "no limit per surface" in forward+? do you just try your best to ignore the overhead it introduces? anyway, my suggestion is add like a "no decal limit per surface" in project settings and leave it off by default so if people need a lot of decals they can enable it and accept performance loss, like in my case because i have a reasonably beefy laptop but opengl still runs smoother than vulkan so for my usecase i think i could just deal with said performance loss. also this is my first ever comment on github so dont kill me pls :3

I'm sorry but I don't think this should be officially supported as a usecase. It adds complexity for the sake of bending the compat rendering to be higher end than it is. In no time we'd have people turning the limit off and then complaining it runs bad.

I am glad this was implemented and I tested it out in Godot 4.8 Beta 1.  

Under use cases like bullet hole decals on a wall, subdividing the wall into many meshes introduces decal clipping because one mesh might be at the max 8 decal per mesh limit, and the other is drawn becuase it not at the limit.

I created a video explaining the limitations with the use case of a machine gun firing at 60 rounds per second.

https://youtu.be/mcV4-2ymtlU

What is more expensive here?  Can the mesh limit be bumped up but still enforce the per frame limit?  Is 32 decals per mesh a problem even if the 64 default max per frame is enforced?
